entries.finding: wary called 'closer to rigid than opposite to it'
entries.reason: Wary and rigid describe different qualities; the comparison is loose and could mislead.
entries.change: A line now says wary means cautious or suspicious, which is not the same as accepting views different from your own.

entries.finding: conceited glossed as 'wants attention'; exam tip generalises to all self- adjectives
entries.reason: Conceited means thinking too highly of yourself, not attention-seeking; words like self-employed break the tip's rule.
entries.change: Dropped 'and wants attention' from the principle; exam tip now scoped to words describing how a person sees themselves.

entries.finding: 'Meetings are not dismissed' absolute; suspended glossed as 'stopped before the business is finished'
entries.reason: Unscoped absolute (check 11); suspension is a temporary pause to resume later, which is the real clash with a finished agenda.
entries.change: Hint 2 and A/B lines: dismissed is used mostly for people or cases and is not the usual word for closing a meeting; suspended means paused for a while, to carry on later.

entries.finding: 'each kind of animal has its own' collective noun
entries.reason: Unscoped absolute; group words overlap (flock and herd of goats) and not every animal has one.
entries.change: Principle now says many kinds of animal have their own group word, and herd is the usual one for cows.

entries.finding: artefact defined as 'a small object'
entries.reason: Artefacts are not necessarily small; the definition is wrong as stated.
entries.change: Hint 2 and B line: an artefact usually names a handmade object such as a tool or pot, not the usual word for a landmark building.

entries.finding: revived glossed only as brought back from fainting or near death, 'too strong for a holiday'
entries.reason: Revive also means restore strength or energy, so 'too strong' is not accurate; the real reason is the natural pairing with refreshed.
entries.change: Hint 3 and B line: revived is most often used for bringing someone round after fainting or collapse; 'refreshed and rejuvenated' is the natural pair.

entries.finding: hint 1: 'Specialist doctors are named after the part of the body they treat'
entries.reason: Unscoped absolute; gynaecologist and paediatrician are named after patient groups. The solution already said 'Many'.
entries.change: Hint 1 now reads 'Many specialist doctors are named after the part of the body or the group of patients they treat'.

entries.finding: hint 3 defines offer, then asks for 'a reward that pushes someone to do more'
entries.reason: Hint 3 as written defines incentive, so it makes the choice for the student.
entries.change: Hint 3 now sends the student back to the purpose clause to decide which of the two words that purpose defines.

entries.finding: broadcast glossed as 'the act' not the programme; prediction 'not the word used with weather'
entries.reason: A broadcast is also the programme itself, and 'weather prediction' is valid English; the point is that 'weather forecast' is the set phrase.
entries.change: Hint 2, B and C lines reworded. Kept 'The other words do not form this set phrase', which is true.

entries.finding: hints 2 and 3 name 'romance' so only one option survives
entries.reason: With romance named in hint 2 and asked for again in hint 3, the choice is made for the student.
entries.change: Hint 2 now describes a sudden, powerful feeling towards a person; hint 3 asks which option matches the strength of 'completely swept off her feet'.

entries.finding: hint 3 'one is vague, the other gives an exact place' gives away D
entries.reason: Form alone points to D without interpreting 'last but one'.
entries.change: Hint 3 now asks the student to count back one place from the last building and match that position.

entries.finding: grandiose line reads as 'not pleasant to look at'
entries.reason: The line can be read as saying grandiose buildings are unattractive, which is false.
entries.change: A line: grandiose is about size and show, not about being pleasant to look at.

entries.finding: C line asserts 'he did not forget anything'
entries.reason: The sentence does not establish that; only that the idiom is not about forgetting.
entries.change: C line: the idiom is not about forgetting; it means someone else used his tactics against him.

entries.finding: placement should be idioms.phrasal-verbs
entries.reason: The taxonomy's two sorting rules conflict here: idioms.idioms claims the 'This means that' format and 'most of WASSCE 2024 Q21 to Q30', while idioms.phrasal-verbs claims any verb and particle. The draft already carries a placement_challenge naming exactly this. Placement belongs to the classifier and adjudication, not the teaching fixer, and the teaching reads correctly under either id.
entries.change: No change; subtopic_id and placement_challenge kept for adjudication.

entries.finding: noticed glossed as 'something a person does with their eyes'
entries.reason: People notice sounds, smells and facts too.
entries.change: A line: noticed is something a person does, seeing or becoming aware of something.

entries.finding: delayed: 'the owner still gets the goods later'
entries.reason: Unscoped claim; delay does not guarantee delivery.
entries.change: B line: delayed means held up or made late, not officially taken away and kept.

entries.finding: lately glossed as 'in the past few days'
entries.reason: Lately covers the recent past generally, not only a few days.
entries.change: B line: lately means recently, in the recent past.

entries.finding: hint 1 says a shorter word is hidden inside inquisitive
entries.reason: No such word is literally inside inquisitive; inquire is a word-family link.
entries.change: Hint 1 now points to words in the same family, such as inquire.

entries.finding: exam tip: a semicolon always means the second part explains the marked word
entries.reason: A semicolon joins related clauses but does not by itself signal an example; the tip was an unscoped rule.
entries.change: Exam tip scoped to cases where the words after the semicolon or 'for example' give an example of the marked word.

entries.finding: hint 2 claims 'the crowd saw the criminal coming'; tip calls menace a word inside menacingly
entries.reason: The sentence does not say the crowd saw him, and menace is not literally inside menacingly (the e drops).
entries.change: Hint 2 now contrasts hiding with showing danger; exam tip now speaks of the base word, allowing for spelling changes.

entries.finding: backshift and 'by then needs the perfect' stated as compulsory; will finish/would finish said to lose completion
entries.reason: Backshift is the usual pattern, not compulsory, and 'would finish by then' can express completion in ordinary English. The real fault of C and D is dropping the perfect form of the original words.
entries.change: Hint 2, principle and exam tip scoped with 'usually' / 'the usual pattern in these questions'; C and D lines now say they drop the perfect form of the original 'will have finished'. Answer and hint 3 unchanged.

entries.finding: 'were' for every subject stated for all unreal conditions
entries.reason: Only true when the verb needed is 'be'; other unreal conditions use knew, had and so on.
entries.change: Principle and exam tip scoped to an if-clause that needs a form of 'be'.

entries.finding: backshift and time/place shifts stated as universal; B said to copy the words 'with no changes at all'
entries.reason: Unscoped absolutes (check 11); the stem already changed I to he, so B's line was imprecise.
entries.change: Hint 2 and principle scoped with 'usually'; B line now says it keeps the verb, place word and time word exactly as spoken. Exam tip already said 'Common shifts' and was left.

entries.finding: 'too' said to need a result; tip says choose 'very' if nothing follows
entries.reason: 'Too + adjective' can stand alone ('She was too unhappy'); the real contrast is high degree against excess. The tip as written would mislead.
entries.change: Hint 3, principle, How to tell, B line and exam tip reframed around degree versus excess; a following result is now only a strong sign of 'too'.

entries.finding: hint 3 'which uses the past form of have' is a text-match after hint 2
entries.reason: After hint 2 names had + past participle, hint 3 let the student scan for 'had' without thinking.
entries.change: Hint 3 now contrasts tying the eating to the present with placing it before 'arrived' and asks which order the sentence needs.

entries.finding: hint 3 says 'the last option', which points to D, already ruled out
entries.reason: Misdirection: the intended comparison is B against C, and 'says the action was wrong' does not describe D.
entries.change: Hint 3 now names 'ought not to' in place of 'the last option'.

entries.finding: exam tip 'keep the first noun singular and plain' stated as a rule
entries.reason: Real exceptions exist (sports car, customs officer); the solution already said 'usually' and the tip should match.
entries.change: Exam tip now says the first noun usually stays singular and plain.

entries.finding: cloze passage Q71 to Q80 read together for sibling leaks
entries.reason: No hint names or defines a sibling's key. Q77 hint 3 mentions the register being checked, but Q78 asks for the name of that check and its own hint 1 already calls it a check. Q79 hints describe officials by stage without naming the announcing step asked in Q80. Other sections share only a section instruction, not content.

entries.finding: revived described as 'most often used for bringing someone round after fainting or collapse'
entries.reason: Revived is commonly used for regaining strength or energy generally (the tea revived her), so the frequency claim is wrong and the stated reason for rejecting B is not the real distinction. The real distinction is that rejuvenated adds the sense of feeling young again.
entries.change: Hint 3 and the B line of Why not the others reworded to describe revived as a general word for getting back strength or energy, with rejuvenated adding the sense of feeling young again. Hint 3 still leaves the choice to the student.

entries.finding: hint 3 defines all three remaining options in option order
entries.reason: The three meanings are listed in the same order as B, C, D, so a student can map them by position and read off the answer without knowing the words. The standard asks hint 3 to narrow to two.
entries.change: Hint 3 now rules out lately and leaves the student to choose between presently and finally.

entries.finding: hint 3's 'If I ___ you' lets the student fill the gap from a memorised idiom
entries.reason: 'If I were you' is a stock phrase, so the example hands over the form for this blank without any reasoning about the unreal condition.
entries.change: Hint 3 now contrasts the ordinary past tense of 'be' with the subjunctive form used with every subject, and asks the student which is which, with no model sentence.

entries.finding: '(The paper printed C and D with the same wording.)' states an unverified claim about the source paper
entries.reason: We only know that C and D are identical in our item data, not what the original paper printed, so the sentence should describe the item as given. The proposed replacement option D 'prices' tag' was rejected because it is a guess and would change the item's option text. The settled answer B is correct whatever D was, so no hold is needed.
entries.change: D line now reads: 'in this version of the question it has the same wording as C, so it fails for the same reason, a plural first noun.' Option text left unchanged.

entries.finding: sibling leaks across passage english-language-wassce-2024-s10 (Q43, Q67)
entries.reason: The hints for Q43 and Q67 cover unrelated points (subjunctive, noun modifiers), and neither gives away another item's answer in the group. Q16 and Q37 are the only draft items from their own groups.

entries.finding: absolutes and scoping reviewed on all four items
entries.reason: No unscoped absolutes found. Q67 already hedges with 'usually', Q43 scopes 'were' to standard written English and WASSCE, and Q43 D is scoped to 'modern English'.
